summary: Describes where RDMAP and DDP apply. It compares transport options for DDP, advises upper layer developers on choosing among them, and compares DDP with direct use of the transports and with non-IP RDMA. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A guide that helps pick which road to use when sending data fast.

questions: what are tagged and untagged messages in ddp
subtitle: A guide to when RDMA and direct data placement over IP are worth using, and how to choose between SCTP and TCP underneath.

tldr.problem: Application and protocol designers need to know when RDMAP and DDP actually help compared with using TCP or SCTP directly, and which transport to run them over.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through tagged and untagged messages, RDMA Reads and ULP credits, then compares DDP over SCTP and over MPA/TCP, and against non-IP RDMA fabrics such as InfiniBand.
tldr.outcome: It is guidance, not a protocol: the benefits are largest for applications designed to exploit them, and the choice of transport is left to the upper layer protocol. It is Informational and has been updated.

today: RFC 5045 is an Informational RFC and is updated by RFC 7146. It gives guidance rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: What RDMAP and DDP Offer
sections.content:
The Remote Direct Memory Access Protocol (RDMAP, RFC 5040) and Direct Data Placement (DDP, RFC 5041) work together to put application payload straight into buffers specified by the Upper Layer Protocol (ULP). DDP does the placement. RDMAP provides completion notifications and RDMA Reads, which let the data receiver fetch from an advertised buffer. DDP can run over IP transports including SCTP and TCP.

This document is about applicability: when these capabilities beat application-specific solutions built directly on the transport, and which transport to pick. It also says the full capabilities are only realized by applications designed to exploit them.
sections.eli5: Normally data arrives in a pile and has to be sorted into the right boxes. Here the sender drops each piece straight into the right box.

sections.title: Tagged and Untagged Messages
sections.content:
A Tagged Message is directed to a ULP-specified buffer by addressing information inside it: the sender chooses the destination, identified by a Steering Tag (STag). The receiver gets no separate notice that it arrived. An Untagged Message is matched against a buffer that the receiver supplied in advance, and the receiver is notified.

Buffer details are shared by an Advertisement: the STag, base address and length. RDMA/DDP leaves how to do this to the ULP, typically inside a Send message. The data source is the Data Source and the receiver is the Data Sink.

Typically tagged data carries payload and untagged messages carry control. No ULP can be defined using only Tagged Messages, because some notification that confirms delivery must come from the RDMAP/DDP layer.
sections.eli5: A tagged message is a parcel with the exact shelf written on it by the sender. An untagged message is a parcel that goes to whichever shelf the receiver set aside and rings the doorbell.

sections.title: Benefits for Data Transfer
sections.content:
Tagged messages let the Data Source choose the order and packetization of delivery, so they can be received out of order without intermediate buffering. RDMAP also consolidates notifications: completion of Tagged Messages is folded into the completion of a trailing Untagged Message, reducing ULP interactions, which matters on high-speed links. The downside is that a ULP cannot start work on an exchange until the whole exchange has been placed, so applications wanting to process each packet promptly may prefer the transport directly.

A typical exchange has five steps: the client sends a request as an untagged message with buffer advertisements; the server sends tagged messages to those buffers; the server sends the reply as an untagged message; the client gets a single notification of completion.

RDMA Reads let a sink fetch just the part of a peer's advertised buffer it needs, just in time. This suits a storage server that wants to limit write buffers per session. It is less suitable when the ULP must run consistency checks, because neither RDMAP nor DDP can bundle several updates atomically.

DDP defines no standard flow control and assumes a ULP mechanism, such as credits allowing a number of Untagged Messages. System buffering from TCP or SCTP can be preferable when pinning many target buffers would be undesirable or when the size of each incoming packet is unknown, as with variable bit rate streaming media.
sections.eli5: The sender can fill your boxes in any order, and you only get one ring of the doorbell when everything is done. That is great if you want the whole delivery, but not if you wanted to start unpacking right away.

sections.title: Choosing Between SCTP and MPA/TCP
sections.content:
Normally the transport is irrelevant to the ULP, because RDMAP and DDP provide the same services over either. There can still be performance differences, and choosing is the ULP's responsibility. SCTP preserves message boundaries; with TCP this needs the MPA (Marker PDU Alignment) adaptation layer. SCTP also has multi-streaming: one association can carry several DDP streams, and per-stream sequence numbers mean a dropped packet for one stream does not delay completions on the others.

MPA/TCP traffic looks like a normal TCP connection to middleboxes, which can matter where only TCP is allowed. It needs more processing than SCTP, which may be justified where SCTP is not fully supported or middleboxes impair it. Both adaptations give end-to-end CRC32c protection. MPA/TCP implementations must implement CRC32c but may turn it off by administrative configuration, only when equivalent end-to-end protection exists; SCTP always provides it. CRC32c guards against random corruption, not forgery, so IPsec is specified for security.

For session setup, both SCTP and MPA allow ULP Private Data before DDP traffic starts, limited to a maximum of 512 bytes. With MPA/TCP, the end that started the conversion to MPA mode must send the first DDP Segment. A transport-neutral ULP should require the initiating end to send first.
sections.eli5: There are two roads, SCTP and TCP with a helper layer. Both reach the same place. One keeps your parcels neatly separated, the other looks like all the other traffic on the highway.

sections.title: Limits and Non-IP Alternatives
sections.content:
Non-IP fabrics such as InfiniBand integrate RDMA with the transport and so have some technical advantages, for example fencing based on transport-level acks. DDP is layered over an IP transport, so it can be added anywhere on an IP network without middlebox support, but it has no RDMA-layer ack. The only ack at the RDMAP layer is an RDMA Read Response.

As a result a local interface cannot fence outbound messages to guarantee earlier Tagged Messages were placed first. Re-use of Tagged Buffers needs extreme care, and the best strategy is to change the state of an advertised buffer only with Untagged Messages. Applications needing stronger ordering must provide it through ULP interaction.

DDP is compatible with an unreliable transport, but RDMAP requires the lower layer to give reliable service. With no transport flow control, RDMAP/DDP would be limited only by the link layer rate, almost inevitably causing severe congestion. Full use also needs a local interface that explicitly requests these services, such as the Sockets Direct Protocol (SDP).
sections.eli5: The special express lanes in other systems have built-in confirmations. On this road you have to ask the other side to tell you when a delivery has really arrived.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
General RDMA security is covered in RFC 5042; this document deals with usage and the effect of the transport choice. Existing methods of filtering, validating and logging the far end of a connection or association still work.

DDP exposes ULP memory only as far as ULP actions allow: posting receives and enabling STags. Enforcement is likely limited to the whole enabled range, and nothing reports if a peer writes into the wrong advertised buffer. Without mutual trust, the receiver might use a distinct STag per interaction and invalidate it after use. Streaming ciphers such as TLS may limit DDP's benefit because they must decrypt in order, while IPsec and DTLS beneath TCP or SCTP do not preclude out-of-order placement.
sections.eli5: Only open the boxes you mean to open, and lock each one after use unless you trust the sender. Some locks make you open parcels in order, which slows the express lane.
